body:
Two different forms of Arab contact

Contacts between Arabia and the Indian subcontinent were established through maritime trade before the Arab conquest of Sindh. Arab sailors and merchants travelled across the Arabian Sea and participated in the exchange of goods between the western Indian coast, West Asia and wider trading networks.

From the 7th century, the spread of Islam added another dimension to these contacts. Muslim merchants and migrants carried their religious traditions as they travelled and settled in coastal communities.

It is essential to distinguish commercial and cultural contact from military conquest. The presence of Arab traders at an Indian port did not automatically mean that an Arab state governed the surrounding territory.

The Arabian Sea trade connection

Western India was well placed for commercial contact with Arabia and the Persian Gulf. Coastal regions of Gujarat and the Malabar coast participated in the wider maritime exchange of commodities, people and ideas.

Trade created opportunities for merchants and coastal settlements. It also allowed religious and cultural traditions to move along existing commercial routes. These developments did not require an army to conquer every port where merchants conducted business.

The Arab conquest of Sindh

The most important early Arab military conquest in the north-western subcontinent occurred in 711–712 CE. Under the Umayyad Caliphate, the commander Muhammad bin Qasim led a campaign into Sindh, in present-day Pakistan.

The local ruler, Raja Dahir, was defeated. Important centres affected by the campaign included Debal and areas farther inland, while Arab authority subsequently extended to centres including Multan.

The conquest brought parts of Sindh under Arab political control. However, it did not establish Arab government throughout India. Independent regional kingdoms continued to exist in Gujarat, Rajasthan, the Deccan and other parts of the subcontinent.

Causes and consequences

The campaign was part of the wider expansion of Arab political power during the early centuries of Islam. Military and political objectives operated alongside the commercial connections already present across the Arabian Sea.

In the areas brought under Arab authority, new political and administrative relationships developed. Meanwhile, commercial exchanges with India's western coast continued through maritime networks that extended beyond the territory actually conquered.

The broader consequence was not a complete replacement of regional Indian political systems. Rather, Arab contact contributed to continuing trade and cultural interactions, while Arab territorial rule remained concentrated in parts of the north-west.

Resistance farther east: the Gujarat connection

Arab armies also attempted to expand beyond Sindh. An important example is the conflict near Navsari in approximately 738–739 CE, when an Arab advance was defeated by forces led by the Chalukya officer Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin.

This event is important for understanding that the Arab conquest of Sindh was followed by military resistance elsewhere. It also provides a direct connection with the history of Gujarat.

Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin of the Navsari victory should not be confused with Pulakeshin II, the earlier Chalukya ruler associated with resistance to Harshavardhana near the Narmada.

What the chronology establishes

Arab maritime interaction with the subcontinent preceded and continued alongside military campaigns. The conquest of Sindh occurred in the early 8th century. The much later campaigns of Mahmud of Ghazni and Muhammad Ghori belonged to different political powers and different centuries.

Therefore, Muhammad bin Qasim, Mahmud of Ghazni and Muhammad Ghori must be treated as 3 distinct historical figures.

Prelims focus

  • Arab maritime trade with India existed before the conquest of Sindh.
  • Muhammad bin Qasim led the Arab conquest of Sindh in 711–712 CE.
  • Raja Dahir was the ruler defeated during the Arab conquest.
  • Sindh and Multan are important places associated with early Arab expansion.
  • Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin is associated with resistance to an Arab advance near Navsari around 738–739 CE.
  • Trap: Arab trade along the western coast did not mean that the whole western coast was conquered by Arab armies.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, ch. 1, 'Tracing Changes Through a Thousand Years', printed p. 12; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, ch. 11, 'New Empires and Kingdoms', printed p. 120; IGNOU, BHIM-162, Unit 4, 'Islamic Invasions and Bharatiya States (8th–12th Century CE)', section on the Arab conquest of Sindh and resistance in western India, printed pp. 77–79 (online, consulted 19 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: Maritime trade linked Arabia with Gujarat and Malabar before conquest; Muhammad bin Qasim’s 711–712 CE campaign brought rule to parts of Sindh, not all India.
pictures.caption: Arab maritime contact and territorial conquest were different developments.

title: Arab Contacts with India: Maritime Trade and the Conquest of Sindh

body:
The Ghaznavid kingdom

Mahmud of Ghazni ruled from 997 to 1030 CE. His capital was Ghazni, in present-day Afghanistan. He expanded Ghaznavid power into parts of Central Asia, Iran and the north-western Indian subcontinent.

Mahmud is especially remembered for repeated military expeditions into India. These expeditions included attacks on wealthy towns and temples, as well as campaigns intended to strengthen political control over north-western territories.

The Ghaznavid kingdom was different from the earlier Umayyad power responsible for the conquest of Sindh. It was also different from the later Ghurid power associated with Muhammad Ghori.

Why Mahmud undertook expeditions

Military expeditions could provide wealth, strengthen political authority and allow a ruler to reward soldiers and maintain his court. Wealthy religious establishments sometimes possessed valuable objects and accumulated resources, making them attractive targets during warfare.

Mahmud's campaigns combined military and political ambitions with the acquisition of wealth. However, the territorial consequences were not identical everywhere he fought.

Parts of the north-west came under lasting Ghaznavid authority, while raids into more distant regions did not necessarily produce permanent administration there.

A raid and a durable conquest are not the same. A raid may involve attacking a place and withdrawing with resources. A durable conquest requires continuing political and military control. Mahmud's activities included both territorial expansion in the north-west and attacks on distant wealthy centres.

The attack on Somnath

One of Mahmud's most famous campaigns was the raid on the Somnath temple in Gujarat, generally dated to 1025–1026 CE.

Somnath was a prominent religious centre on the Saurashtra coast. Mahmud's attack formed part of his repeated campaigns against wealthy targets. The expedition was followed by his withdrawal rather than the establishment of lasting Ghaznavid rule over all of Gujarat.

The campaign occurred during the period of Bhima I of the Chaulukya or Solanki dynasty of Gujarat. The contemporaneous ruler and the attacking ruler must be distinguished: Bhima I belonged to the regional Gujarat dynasty, while Mahmud ruled from Ghazni.

Ghazni as a centre of power and learning

Wealth acquired through campaigns helped Mahmud support an important royal centre at Ghazni. His court also attracted learned figures, including Al-Biruni.

Al-Biruni studied Indian intellectual and social traditions and produced an influential Arabic account known as Kitab ul-Hind, also called Tahqiq-i-Hind. He drew on discussions with learned people and the study of Sanskrit works.

The association should be remembered accurately: Mahmud was the Ghaznavid ruler; Al-Biruni was a scholar. The book is associated with the intellectual environment of the Ghaznavid period, not with a military victory by its author.

What Mahmud's campaigns changed

Ghaznavid expansion strengthened its hold over important parts of the north-western subcontinent. Repeated attacks also affected the security and resources of the regions targeted.

Nevertheless, Mahmud did not establish the Delhi Sultanate. That political development followed the later Ghurid conquests and the rise of commanders who established authority in northern India.

Prelims focus

  • Mahmud of Ghazni ruled from 997 to 1030 CE.
  • His capital was Ghazni, in present-day Afghanistan.
  • The Somnath raid in Gujarat is generally dated to 1025–1026 CE.
  • Bhima I was the Gujarat Chaulukya ruler associated with the period of the Somnath raid.
  • Al-Biruni authored Kitab ul-Hind, an Arabic account of India.
  • Trap: Mahmud of Ghazni did not found the Delhi Sultanate.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, ch. 2, 'New Kings and Kingdoms', printed pp. 20–21; GCERT, History, Class 11, ch. 12, 'Medieval India', section on Al-Biruni and his writings; GCERT, Social Science, Class 7, ch. 1, 'Rajput Age: New Ruler and States', section on Gujarat; IGNOU, BHIM-162, Unit 4, 'Islamic Invasions and Bharatiya States (8th–12th Century CE)', section on the Ghaznavid campaigns (online, consulted 19 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: Mahmud held parts of the north-west, but the Somnath raid of 1025–1026 CE ended in withdrawal, without lasting rule over all Gujarat.
pictures.caption: Mahmud's campaigns combined northwestern territorial control with raids farther into India.

title: Mahmud of Ghazni: Northwestern Expansion and the Somnath Raid

body:
The rise of the Ghurids

The Ghurids were a ruling power associated with Ghor, in the region of present-day Afghanistan. Their important ruler Muizz al-Din Muhammad is commonly known as Muhammad Ghori or Muhammad of Ghor.

His campaigns in the late 12th century differed in their political consequences from many of Mahmud of Ghazni's earlier raids. Ghurid commanders established military positions and developed control over territories that later became important to the Delhi Sultanate.

Early campaigns and the defeat in Gujarat

Muhammad Ghori began campaigns towards the north-western subcontinent in the 1170s. An expedition against Multan took place in 1175 CE.

In 1178 CE, he attempted to advance into Gujarat but was defeated by forces of the Chaulukya or Solanki kingdom. The battle is associated with Kasahrada or Kayadra, near the Mount Abu region.

This defeat is important for 2 reasons. It demonstrates the ability of a regional Indian kingdom to resist the Ghurid advance, and it helps explain why subsequent Ghurid expansion placed greater emphasis on routes through Punjab.

The Gujarat event must not be confused with Mahmud of Ghazni's much earlier Somnath raid. The 2 campaigns were separated by more than a century and involved different rulers.

The move towards Punjab

Muhammad Ghori subsequently concentrated on the north-western approaches to the Ganga plain. In 1186 CE, he took Lahore, ending the remaining Ghaznavid ruling position there.

Control of Lahore strengthened the Ghurid position in Punjab. It also provided a more secure base for further campaigns towards important northern Indian political centres.

The 2 battles of Tarain

The Chahamana ruler Prithviraja III, commonly called Prithviraj Chauhan, controlled an important kingdom associated with Ajmer and the Delhi region. He confronted Muhammad Ghori near Tarain, in the area of present-day Haryana.

First Battle of Tarain, 1191

In 1191 CE, Prithviraja III defeated Muhammad Ghori. This was a victory for the Chahamana side and a setback to Ghurid expansion.

Second Battle of Tarain, 1192

In 1192 CE, Muhammad Ghori returned and defeated Prithviraja III. The result seriously weakened Chahamana power in the Delhi region and opened the way for wider Ghurid expansion in northern India.

Tarain, 1191: Prithviraja III defeated Muhammad Ghori.
Tarain, 1192: Muhammad Ghori defeated Prithviraja III.

The outcome of the second battle was historically important because Ghurid commanders were subsequently able to extend their influence over strategic centres. However, a single battle did not instantly bring every part of northern India under one administration.

The Battle of Chandawar, 1194

In 1194 CE, Muhammad Ghori defeated Jayachandra, the Gahadavala ruler associated with Kanauj and Varanasi, at the Battle of Chandawar.

This victory weakened another important regional kingdom and facilitated further Ghurid expansion in the Ganga plain.

The major campaigns compared

YearEventKey result
1175Campaign towards MultanEarly Ghurid advance into the north-west
1178Campaign in GujaratDefeat by Chaulukya forces near Kasahrada or Kayadra
1186Capture of LahoreEnd of remaining Ghaznavid rule there
1191First Battle of TarainPrithviraja III defeated Muhammad Ghori
1192Second Battle of TarainMuhammad Ghori defeated Prithviraja III
1194Battle of ChandawarMuhammad Ghori defeated Jayachandra

From Ghurid conquest to the Delhi Sultanate

After the Ghurid victories, military commanders administered and defended important territories. Qutb al-Din Aibak was among Muhammad Ghori's leading commanders in India.

Following Muhammad Ghori's death in 1206, Aibak established independent authority, marking the beginning of the Delhi Sultanate. Thus, the Ghurid conquests prepared the ground for the Sultanate, but Muhammad Ghori himself should not be identified as the first Sultan of Delhi.

Prelims focus

  • Muhammad Ghori is also known as Muizz al-Din Muhammad.
  • He was defeated by Chaulukya forces in Gujarat in 1178 CE.
  • He captured Lahore in 1186 CE.
  • Prithviraja III won the First Battle of Tarain in 1191; Muhammad Ghori won the Second Battle in 1192.
  • At Chandawar in 1194, Muhammad Ghori defeated the Gahadavala ruler Jayachandra.
  • Trap: Muhammad Ghori's conquests preceded the Delhi Sultanate; Qutb al-Din Aibak established independent Sultanate authority in 1206.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, ch. 2, 'New Kings and Kingdoms', printed p. 21; GCERT, Social Science, Class 7, ch. 1, 'Rajput Age: New Ruler and States', sections on the Chauhans and Gujarat; GCERT, History, Class 11, ch. 13, 'Rajput States of India', section on the Chahamanas; UNESCO, History of Civilizations of Central Asia, Volume IV, K. A. Nizami, 'The Ghurids', printed pp. 187–189 (online, consulted 19 November 2026); IGNOU, BHIM-162, Unit 4, 'Islamic Invasions and Bharatiya States (8th–12th Century CE)', section on the Ghurid campaigns, printed pp. 86–89 (online, consulted 19 November 2026).]

pictures.caption: How the Ghurid advance shifted after the Gujarat defeat.

title: Muhammad Ghori: Gujarat, Tarain and the Ghurid Conquests

body:
Why the 3 phases must be distinguished

Three major phases of contact and conquest are commonly studied together: Arab contact and the conquest of Sindh, Mahmud of Ghazni's campaigns, and Muhammad Ghori's conquests. They took place at different times and involved different rulers, political centres and territorial consequences.

The differences are important because a multiple-choice option may correctly name a person but incorrectly connect that person to another century, battle or political outcome.

Ruler, period and territorial effect

PhasePrincipal figure and dateMain place or eventImportant distinction
Arab conquestMuhammad bin Qasim, 711–712Sindh; defeat of Raja DahirEarly territorial conquest, not conquest of all India
Ghaznavid campaignsMahmud of Ghazni, 997–1030North-west; Somnath raid, 1025–1026Northwestern control and repeated raids
Ghurid conquestsMuhammad Ghori, late 12th centuryGujarat, Lahore, Tarain and ChandawarVictories that prepared the way for later Sultanate authority

The difference between trade, raids and political conquest

Trade and settlement

Merchants travel to exchange goods and may establish commercial or residential communities. Trade can spread ideas and religious practices without transferring sovereignty to the merchants' place of origin.

Arab maritime contact with India's western coast is an example of this distinction.

Military raids

A raid involves a military expedition directed against a target, frequently to obtain wealth or weaken an opponent. The attacking army may withdraw without maintaining an administrative presence at that particular place.

Mahmud's attack on Somnath is an example of a campaign that should not be treated as proof of lasting Ghaznavid administration throughout Gujarat.

Territorial conquest

A conquest becomes politically durable when the victorious power establishes continuing military and administrative authority over territory. The Arab conquest of parts of Sindh and the later Ghurid establishment of important positions in northern India provide examples.

These categories can overlap within the history of a single ruler. Mahmud's state gained lasting northwestern territories while also conducting raids farther away. The distinction concerns the outcome in a particular territory, not merely the name of the attacking ruler.

Comparison of the Gujarat connections

Gujarat appears in more than one episode, but each belongs to a different political context:

  • 738–739: The Chalukya officer Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin is associated with resistance to an Arab advance near Navsari.
  • 1025–1026: Mahmud of Ghazni attacked Somnath during the period of the Gujarat Chaulukya ruler Bhima I.
  • 1178: Muhammad Ghori was defeated by Chaulukya forces near Kasahrada or Kayadra.

These episodes should not be combined into one invasion or attributed to one ruling dynasty. The Navsari conflict involved an earlier Chalukya political setting, while Somnath and Kasahrada belonged to the period of the Gujarat Chaulukyas or Solankis.

The importance of accurate place associations

The place named in a question often reveals the correct episode. Sindh points to Muhammad bin Qasim, Somnath to Mahmud's celebrated raid, Kasahrada to Ghori's Gujarat defeat, Tarain to Prithviraja III and Muhammad Ghori, and Chandawar to Muhammad Ghori and Jayachandra.

Prelims focus

  • Muhammad bin Qasim is associated with Sindh in 711–712 CE.
  • Mahmud of Ghazni is associated with Somnath in 1025–1026 CE.
  • Muhammad Ghori is associated with the Gujarat defeat of 1178 CE.
  • Prithviraja III and Muhammad Ghori fought at Tarain in 1191 and 1192.
  • Jayachandra and Muhammad Ghori are associated with Chandawar in 1194.
  • Trap: Arab sea trade, Ghaznavid raids and Ghurid territorial conquests describe different forms of interaction and must not be treated as identical.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, ch. 11, 'New Empires and Kingdoms', printed p. 120; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, ch. 2, 'New Kings and Kingdoms', printed p. 21; IGNOU, BHIM-162, Unit 4, 'Islamic Invasions and Bharatiya States (8th–12th Century CE)', sections on Arab, Ghaznavid and Ghurid campaigns (online, consulted 19 November 2026); UNESCO, History of Civilizations of Central Asia, Volume IV, K. A. Nizami, 'The Ghurids', printed pp. 187–189 (online, consulted 19 November 2026).]

pictures.caption: Three different episodes involving Gujarat and external military powers.

title: Comparing Arab, Ghaznavid and Ghurid Expansion
